population.note: Branded Chrome's built-in default (fresh profile, no flags). latest.json gives no share for it.

No study in the captured variations seed toggles TLSTrustAnchorIDs, so latest.json has no population figure; branded Chrome drops ca34 only with --disable-features=TLSTrustAnchorIDs (or a future Finch study).
Sum of share_of_population over the study groups that enable AddTLSServerHandshakePadding.

verdict_rules.reference: Chrome's default fingerprint (branded Chrome, fresh profile, no flags; includes ca34)
verdict_rules.exact: 0 counted fields differ from Chrome's default fingerprint
verdict_rules.exact_variant: 0 counted fields differ from one of Chrome's less common variants (without ca34, or the post-quantum experiment), but not the default
verdict_rules.close: exactly 1 counted field differs from the default fingerprint
verdict_rules.behind: 2 or more counted fields differ from the default fingerprint
verdict_rules.versions_behind: Chrome major of the newest fully rolled-out stable (per platform, latest.json current_stable.highest_full_rollout) minus the major in the profile name

caveats: Chrome sends more than one real fingerprint. The default (branded Chrome 154.0.8037.97, fresh profile, no flags) includes the trust-anchors extension ca34; --disable-features=TLSTrustAnchorIDs removes it; and 6% of linux stable clients are in Google's PqcBandwidthExperiment, which adds extension 0x12e0. Every library is compared against all three; the verdict uses the default.
Reference: branded Google Chrome 154.0.8037.97 (stable), captured Oct 6, 2026 on Linux x86_64 against a local capture server (capture/lib/server.py).
No population figure exists in the capture for Chrome without ca34 (no Finch study in the seed toggles it), so none is shown.
HTTP/3: 8 library profiles were tested over QUIC against the same local aioquic endpoint that captured Chrome's QUIC fingerprint; libraries without an HTTP/3 client are marked 'no HTTP/3 support'.
Resumption was only tested for bogdanfinn tls-client (Chrome_152 and Chrome_152_PSK).
Header order is informational: the harness sets Chrome headers for the Go libraries, while Python cases use each library's defaults.
Verdicts compare against the Linux Chrome capture. Windows and macOS Chrome are captured separately and shown next to Linux; libraries are not scored against them.
